runlength_smear — 2D morphology op

• Data kinds: image → image

• Call: fullseye.apply(img, "runlength_smear", a=0.5, b=0.5) (the 2-D model is one image plus two scalar knobs a,b∈[0,1])

*The 4th column is a colour (H,W,3) input. This op handles colour without crossing channels (it does not convolve the colour channel as a third spatial axis).*

Usage

Run-length smoothing (RLSA). Fills the gaps between characters within a line and merges the characters into "line" blocks.

A basic building block of page layout analysis (which parts are lines, which are columns). a sweeps the length of the gaps to fill over 3,5,9,15,25,41,65 pixels (a line along the direction given by b), and b selects the direction and the

combination: b <= 0.5 is horizontal only, 0.5 < b <= 0.75 is vertical only, b > 0.75 is the smaller of horizontal and vertical (= the 2-pass AND combination of classic RLSA. Only places filled in both directions remain, so not just lines but column blocks emerge).

★Partly overlaps the existing gclose. gclose can select a horizontal-line structuring element via b, so horizontal RLSA can be written with it in principle. What this op adds is 2 things ——

(1) the gap can be swept up to 65 pixels rather than 3–9 (at the upper limit of _k lines do not join up;

the spacing between characters is 10–30 pixels for 96 px glyphs), (2) the AND combination of 2 directions cannot be written as a closing with a single structuring element. For one direction only, gclose is faster.

It applies directly to greyscale images (no internal binarisation). Since it is a grey-level closing, it works in the direction of filling dark gaps —— use it on images with bright characters on a dark background. For the reverse, pass the image through invert first. Border handling is scipy.ndimage's default reflect. An empty frame (constant image) is returned unchanged (there are no gaps to fill). The value range stays as in the input, within [0,1], and there is no per-image normalisation (values are comparable across images).
